## Credit Card Probability of Default {#sec-credit-card}

Under the Basel III IRB Advanced Approach, probability-of-default (PD) models must satisfy two simultaneous criteria: ranking quality (correctly ordering borrowers by risk) and probability calibration (predicted default rates must track observed frequencies across rating grades) [@eba_gl_2017_16; @iasb_ifrs9_2014; @basel_committee_basel_2011]. GP-based methods have been applied to credit-risk problems [@mahajan_gaussian_2022; @huang_using_2011], but their native calibration advantage over classical models has not been directly quantified at scale. We therefore evaluate whether GP and DGP classifiers satisfy these regulatory criteria on a realistic credit-risk benchmark, and whether DGP depth adds any discriminative value over a single-layer GP on this smooth financial surface.

The benchmark is the UCI default of credit card clients dataset [@yeh_comparisons_2009], comprising 30,000 observations and 23 predictor variables: credit limit, demographics, six months of repayment-status history, and corresponding billing and repayment amounts from April–September 2005. The target indicates default on the October 2005 payment. This benchmark is commonly used in existing credit-risk literature [@thomas_survey_2000; @huang_using_2011; @mahajan_gaussian_2022] and presents two simultaneous evaluation criteria: ranking quality (does the model correctly order clients by default risk?) and probability calibration (are the predicted default probabilities credible estimates of observed default frequencies?).

#### Data Preparation and Experimental Design

Undocumented education and marriage codes were collapsed into an "other" category, skewed monetary variables (bill amounts and repayment amounts) were log-transformed to reduce leverage from extreme values, categorical variables were one-hot encoded with `drop_first=True`, and all continuous predictors were standardised to zero mean and unit variance fit on the training split only to prevent leakage (see @sec-credit-risk-preprocessing-snippet for the implementation). The full 30,000-observation dataset was first split into a fixed held-out test set of 6,000 observations (20%), stratified by the target variable to ensure equal default rates across all splits.
The remaining 24,000 observations form the development pool. This ensures all models across sizes are evaluated on the same test set, giving a fair comparison across training-set sizes.

- Small: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 500$): 425 training, 75 validation observations.
- Medium: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 5{,}000$): 4,250 training, 750 validation observations.
- Large: ($N_{\text{dev}} = 24{,}000$): 20,400 training, 3,600 validation observations (full development set).

The validation split (15% of dev) is used only for XGBoost early stopping; all other models train on the full train+validation set after hyperparameter selection, following the convention for small-data GP experiments in @hensman_gaussian_2013. The test set default rate is 22.1% across all tiers.

#### Model Set and Training Configuration {#sec-uci-models}

The model set and training protocol are consistent with @sec-kin8nm, adapted for binary classification with a Bernoulli likelihood. Three classical baselines are used: logistic regression (replacing Ridge regression from Kin8nm for the classification setting), random forest, and XGBoost. The same three GP-family models are used: SVGP, DSVGP-2L, and DSVGP-3L. All models are trained at each of the three training set sizes (small, medium, large) to characterise scaling behaviour.

| Logistic Regression | 0.739 | 0.493 | 0.513 | 0.55 | 0.225 | 0.199 | 0.590 | 0.03 |
| Random Forest | 0.769 | 0.549 | 0.538 | 0.40 | 0.087 | 0.146 | 0.460 | 4.57 |
| XGBoost | **0.779** | **0.553** | 0.543 | 0.55 | 0.196 | 0.177 | 0.539 | 0.58 |
| SVGP | 0.776 | 0.551 | **0.546** | 0.30 | **0.015** | **0.136** | **0.432** | 149.7 |
| DSVGP-2L | 0.778 | 0.548 | 0.541 | 0.30 | 0.017 | **0.135** | **0.430** | 186.1 |

: Model comparison at full scale ($N_{\text{train}} = 20{,}400$, $N_{\text{test}} = 6{,}000$). All threshold-dependent metrics reported at each model's F1-optimal threshold $t^*$. Bold entries indicate leading values. {#tbl-uci-large}

![ROC and precision-recall curves at full scale. XGBoost narrowly leads on ROC-AUC (0.779); GP-family models form the second group at 0.776–0.778.](/sections/4-modeling/assets/credit-card-default/large/roc_pr.png){#fig-uci-large-roc-pr}

![Reliability diagrams at full scale. GP-family models track the diagonal closely (ECE $\leq 0.017$); logistic regression and XGBoost show substantial miscalibration (ECE $> 0.19$).](/sections/4-modeling/assets/credit-card-default/large/calibration.png){#fig-uci-large-calibration}

XGBoost leads on ROC-AUC (0.779) and average precision (0.553), with the GP family following at 0.776–0.778 — a gap within the $\pm 0.015$ bootstrap CI, making the top four models statistically indistinguishable on discrimination (@sec-appendix-uci-ci). At F1-optimal thresholds, performance converges: SVGP = 0.546 ($t^* = 0.30$), XGBoost = 0.543 ($t^* = 0.55$). GP models' lower optimal thresholds (0.30 vs 0.40–0.55 for classical models) reflect narrower posterior score distributions — a consequence of principled uncertainty quantification rather than a deficiency.

The standout result is **probability calibration**: GP models achieve ECE = 0.015–0.017 versus 0.087–0.225 for classical baselines — a 5–13$\times$ improvement requiring no post-hoc calibration [@niculescu_mizil_predicting_2005]. Under Basel IRB, PD estimates must track observed default rates across rating grades [@eba_gl_2017_16]; XGBoost's ECE of 0.196 would fail supervisory review, whereas GP models satisfy this standard natively, avoiding the additional validation burden of Platt scaling [@platt_probabilistic_1999] or isotonic regression under SR 11-7 [@federal_reserve_sr11_7].

ROC and precision-recall curves and reliability diagrams at each training tier are provided in @sec-appendix-uci-scaling.

All models improve with more data, but the patterns differ by family. XGBoost shows the strongest discriminative scaling (+0.045 ROC-AUC from small to large), while GP models converge toward XGBoost at large scale. DSVGP-3L collapses at small scale (ROC-AUC = 0.529), a clear instance of the pathological behaviour identified by @duvenaud_avoiding_2014 — overly deep architectures suffer vanishing kernel gradients with limited data. It recovers fully by medium scale.

On calibration, GP models maintain ECE $\leq 0.029$ from 425 training observations onward, while classical models are miscalibrated at all scales. XGBoost ECE actually *worsens* from 0.164 (small) to 0.196 (large) as more confident fits produce more extreme scores without an intrinsic calibration mechanism [@niculescu_mizil_predicting_2005].

#### Computational Profile {#sec-uci-cost}

| Model | Time (s, small) | Time (s, medium) | Time (s, large) |
|:------|:-------:|:-------:|:-------:|
| Logistic Regression | 0.006 | 0.007 | 0.03 |
| Random Forest | 0.45 | 1.13 | 4.57 |
| XGBoost | 0.06 | 0.19 | 0.58 |
| SVGP | 3.5 | 31.4 | 149.7 |
| DSVGP-2L | 3.8 | 36.5 | 186.1 |
| DSVGP-3L | 13.7 | 133.9 | 616.1 |

: Training time scaling across tiers. GP models scale approximately linearly with $N$; DSVGP-3L is $\sim 3.3\times$ the cost of DSVGP-2L at all scales. {#tbl-uci-runtime}

DSVGP-3L is the most expensive model at 616 seconds — approximately 3.3$\times$ the cost of the two-layer variant — yet yields no material improvement over DSVGP-2L on any metric at large scale (ROC-AUC: 0.777 vs 0.778; ECE: 0.016 vs 0.017). This is consistent with @duvenaud_avoiding_2014, who demonstrate that additional GP layers suppress rather than enhance flexibility on smooth finite datasets. DSVGP-2L is consequently the more defensible configuration: it achieves near-best discrimination, excellent calibration, and approximately one-third the training cost of the three-layer variant.

For deployment contexts, the GP training time penalty (186 s for DSVGP-2L vs 0.58 s for XGBoost at large scale — a ${\sim}320\times$ factor) is a batch training cost incurred once per model refresh cycle. In credit-risk production environments where models are retrained monthly or quarterly, this is operationally negligible. Inference time for a single prediction is comparable across model families.

#### Summary {#sec-uci-discussion}

GP and DGP classifiers match XGBoost on discrimination (ROC-AUC within $\pm 0.003$, statistically indistinguishable) while providing 5–13$\times$ better native probability calibration — the property most important for regulatory PD estimation. This calibration advantage holds across all training set sizes, even from 425 observations. DSVGP-2L is the preferred deep configuration: it matches SVGP on all metrics (the +0.002 ROC-AUC difference is not significant), while DSVGP-3L adds ${\sim}3.3\times$ training cost with no measurable gain and fails catastrophically at small scale. The GP training time premium (${\sim}320\times$ vs XGBoost) is a batch cost incurred once per model refresh — operationally negligible in quarterly PD model cycles. The lack of DGP improvement over SVGP is consistent with @sec-kin8nm, confirming that the compositional flexibility of DGPs only yields gains on non-stationary target functions rather than the smooth credit-default surfaces typical of financial risk.
